newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq in diplomatic offensive to ease isolation.
newsitem.headline: Iraq in diplomatic offensive to ease isolation.

text.p: Iraq has launched a fresh diplomatic offensive to ease its political and economic isolation following a partial oil sales deal signed with the United Nations in December.

Senior Iraqi officials started the year by visiting several countries including France and Russia -- both permanent members of the U.N. Security Council -- as well as a number of southeast Asian countries.
"The offensive is two-pronged this time," said a European diplomat. "It is to lure these countries to do business with Baghdad and turn them to Iraq's side in dealing with U.N. demands on weapons."

Under the terms of the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire, Iraq must destroy its arsenal of weapons of mass destruction. It can only resume unrestricted oil sales once it gets a clean bill of health from a United Nations arms commission.
Diplomats say Iraq is trying to win friends abroad because it is at loggerheads with the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) set up by the security council to supervise the arsenal's annihilation.

UNSCOM chairman Rolf Ekeus has said he may withhold granting Iraq a clean bill if his weapons experts are denied access to Baghdad's past weapons programmes, including the long-range missiles it is banned from manufacturing.
A U.N. ballistic missile team is currently working with the Iraqi authorities to determine the whereabouts of these weapons.
Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz was in Paris this month and had separate meetings with Foreign Minister Herve de Charette and Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

Aziz's visit was overshadowed by remarks in the ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra lambasting a decision by France not to allow treatment of President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday on its soil. Uday was shot and wounded in Baghdad on December 12.

But Iraq's most senior diplomat played down the criticism. Praising France for withrawing from allied air patrols protecting rebel Kurds in northern Iraq, he said French companies had snatched the largest share of contracts under the U.N. oil deal worth $2 billion in six months.

A day after his return to Baghdad, 50 French agriculture and food producers displayed their products at Baghdad's al-Rasheed Hotel in the first exhibition of its kind by French firms since sanctions were clamped on Iraq for invading Kuwait in 1990.

To Moscow, Iraq has sent Saad al-Feisal, senior undersecretary at the foreign ministry. Official newspapers said Feisal had met Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov to ask Russia's help to have the oil ban lifted completely.
Parliamentary speaker Saadon Hammadi is on a tour of southeast Asian countries. He has visited Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia and he may drop in on other countries in the region.

But meeting U.N. demands on weapons, though the only condition for free oil sales under the major Gulf War ceasefire resolution, may not mean the end of sanctions for Iraq's ailing economy and impoverished population.
The United States insists on other conditions being met and France mentioned the issue of missing Kuwaitis and Saudis from the Gulf war including other issues during Aziz's visit.
Diplomats in Baghdad said Iraq was trying to make 1997 its final year under U.N. trade sanctions.
Expressing this hope, the government newspaper al- Jumhouriya predicted in a commentary on Saturday that 1997 would "expedite the termination of the unfair embargo".

But diplomats also said Iraqi officials feared the United States and Britain, anti-Iraq hawks on the U.N. Security Council, would make the partial oil sales deal a substitute for the total lifting of the oil embargo.
